sources.name: The Guardian Technology
sources.title: Jensen Huang’s image has been shattered. Could he be pushed out at Nvidia?
sources.text: Huang built Nvidia as a family business but after the co-founder had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, its board faces a difficult decision For more than 30 years, Jensen Huang has been the seemingly unshakable public face of Nvidia. He co-founded the company as a young engineer in 1993 and oversaw its growth into a multitrillion dollar chipmaker and bellwether of the AI industry at large. He’s also made it a family business. His children, Madison and Spencer, have taken leadership roles at the firm. While not a company executive, his wife, Lori Mills Huang, leads the family foundation which, as of 2024, controls over 60m Nvidia shares. But Huang’s image as a family man has been shattered as of Sunday. After the New York Times revealed at the end of October that Huang may have been targeted by a Chinese intelligence asset who he had developed a close relationship with, he admitted in a letter to employees on Sunday that he had been having an affair. Initially , Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said there was nothing out of the ordinary about Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang , an executive at a Singaporean datacenter firm, Megaspeed. US government officials had suspected Huang of smuggling American chips into China, prompting those officials to surveil and monitor her, the Times first reported. In the course of that surveillance, officials allegedly determined that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and had gotten close with the Nvidia leader. Nvidia’s board of directors have now launched an independent investigation about the national security concerns surrounding Huang’s relationship. “I support the investigation and will cooperate fully,” Huang wrote in his letter. “I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.” Megaspeed did not respond to a Guardian request for comment before publication. In his letter, Huang apologized to his family, acknowledging how much they’ve supported him. His wife, Mills, kept a relatively low profile and didn’t play a formal role at Nvidia. However, in a 2023 interview with the New Yorker, Huang shared that Mills had also worked in Silicon Valley as a microchips engineer before stepping away to raise their children. “Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support,” Huang wrote in his letter to employees. “They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.” Both his children now hold high ranking roles at the company, despite not initially pursuing careers in tech. His daughter, Madison, serves as the senior director of product and technical marketing for physical AI platforms, but got her start as a chef. She attended the Culinary Institute of America and Le Cordon Bleu before going to business school and transitioning to luxury marketing. She previously worked at LVMH – the parent company of Lous Vuitton. Spencer , for his part, now serves as the director of product for Robotics at Nvidia but spent much of his career as a consultant before joining his father’s company as a product manager. Before consulting, he owned and co-founded a craft cocktail bar in Taiwan. In his letter, Huang reiterated his commitment to Nvidia, saying he hoped to earn back his colleagues’ and employees’ trust. However, analysts and investors say there’s a chance he may be removed as CEO after the board’s investigation. “This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons,” said Dan Ives, a partner and analyst at investment bank Yorkville Ives. “There is clearly risk as discussed that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the board investigation and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally.” Ives said the family’s role at Nvidia adds some complexities for the board. “The board has to make its decision independent of the family spider web of Jensen and his family at Nvidia,” Ives told the Guardian. “It makes this a very complex situation for the board to navigate with the world watching.” Huang is to Nvidia what Steve Jobs was to Apple, said Ken Mahoney, the CEO and president of Mahoney Asset Management. “If you asked any Nvidia investor or anyone involved in tech and markets, would they like to see Jensen gone? Definitely not, but [Nvidia] would survive,” Mahoney said. “Losing Huang would introduce a lot of uncertainty, particularly given his influence over Nvidia’s strategy, culture, and relationships with major technology companies,” he continued. “The bigger question is whether a successor could maintain Huang’s strategic vision and ability to anticipate where the industry is heading, and how that new leader could be tested along the way if things become difficult.” Executive affairs or inappropriate relationships have recently unseated CEOs, according to executive recruiting and coaching firm Challenger Gray and Christmas. In 2024, the CEO of Astronomer was caught on a kiss cam with the company’s chief people officer, leading him to resign shortly after. Nestlé fired CEO Laurent Freixe for a relationship with a subordinate. Nvidia offers a more complex picture. On one hand, Huang’s affair is not just a matter morals or ethics, there are potential national security concerns. On the other, Huang is core to the DNA of Nvidia which in turn is the bedrock of the entire AI industry – an industry upon which the economy relies greatly. Nvidia shares fell 7.5% as soon as the stock market opened, wiping over $330bn off the company’s value. “When the CEO of the most valuable company in the world is tied to a counterintelligence investigation because of a personal relationship, every board in America should be paying attention,” said

sources.title: Nvidia board member Stephen Neal could play big role in probe of CEO Jensen Huang
sources.text: Nvidia's investigation into CEO Jensen Huang over his affair with an alleged Chinese spy may hinge on decisions by company board member Stephen Neal , a longtime white-collar defense attorney whose extensive resume includes dealing with corporate scandals. Neal, the former CEO of the Cooley law firm, is Nvidia's lead independent director and head of corporate governance. Nvidia has not named the investigators who will probe the allegations surrounding Huang, but the company has said its board is leading the probe with help from outside counsel. Neal's experience makes him a likely key figure in the investigation. Nvidia's board has said there is "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised" by Huang's admitted affair with Alice Huang, who had been an executive with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer. China dismissed U.S. intelligence conclusions that Alice Huang was a spy, which were first reported by The New York Times . Jensen Huang, one of the most powerful businessmen in the artificial intelligence boom, has said he would "cooperate fully" with the investigation. Nvidia's board has 10 independent members, including a former president of Taco Bell , a former Eli Lilly executive, and a former vice chairman from Goldman Sachs . Neal has litigated cases across securities, bankruptcies, antitrust, takeovers and more, according to his Cooley bio. And he's conducted several investigations for multiple boards of directors, including at General Motors , where he advised the company in disputes with Ross Perot. Neal has also conducted several investigations for committees of directors and independent directors, though most of those client names are confidential. He's also handled investigations with the Securities and Exchange Commission for both corporations and individuals. When he joined Nvidia, Neal was also the chairman of the board of directors at Levi Strauss . He stepped down in 2021 after reaching the mandatory board retirement age of 72, the company said at the time. The retailer did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Monday. Neal joined Nvidia's board in 2019. He is chairman emeritus and senior counsel at Cooley, and was the firm's CEO from 2001 to 2008. Neal did not respond to a request for comment from CNBC. Neal's past clients include Elizabeth Holmes , the convicted fraudster who founded the blood-testing startup Theranos, and late financier Charles Keating Jr . Neal and other Cooley lawyers represented Holmes in a class-action civil lawsuit in Arizona federal court over Theranos' blood-testing services, which produced bogus results. In September 2019, Neal and his colleagues asked to be removed from the case because Holmes could not pay their legal bills. A judge granted that withdrawal motion less than two months later. In 1989, Neal was hired to represent Keating, who had become the face of the massive savings and loan scandal in the United States as head of American Continental, which owned the California-based thrift Lincoln Savings & Loan. Keating's campaign contributions to five U.S. senators — none of whom were charged with wrongdoing — earned them the notorious sobriquet "The Keating Five." Keating was sentenced in 1992 to up to 10 years in prison by Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Lance Ito for an extensive fraud. Ito later gained fame as the judge in O.J. Simpson's murder trial. Keating ended up serving less than five years after that conviction and a federal one were overturned on appeal. Neal represented Keating in his efforts to overturn his convictions. In a 1997 article about Keating, Time magazine called Neal "the legal Houdini behind his release." Neal also has ties in and around Silicon Valley. In November 2022, in the wake of the collapse of the $32 billion cryptocurrency firm FTX, the company's founder, Sam Bankman-Fried, nominated Neal to serve as chairman of the board of FTX Trading, the FTX-affiliated hedge fund Alameda Research, and a third affiliate, West Realm Shires, as part of a Chapter 11 bankruptcy petition. But Cooley said Neal was "unable to serve in" those positions, Business Insider reported at the time. Neal received his law degree from Stanford, where Bankman-Fried's parents had been law professors. Neal is also chairperson of the trust for Meta's Oversight Board , which is responsible for examining whether Meta's decisions to remove or leave up content on Facebook, Instagram or Threads were in line with the company's policies and values. And on Tuesday, the journalist Theo Baker, whose articles as a freshman reporter on The Stanford Daily at Stanford University about allegations against that school's president Marc Tessier-Lavinge led to his resignation, said in an X post that Tessier-Lavinge had hired Neal "to try to stop my reporting on allegations of research misconduct from coming out." Cooley's history with Nvidia goes back decades. The law firm said it incorporated the company in 1993 and has served as its principal outside corporate and litigation counsel for roughly three decades. Cooley handled Nvidia's initial public offering in 1999. Investors will be closely watching the investigation, and its emphasis on independence, as the process unfolds, according to Brayden King, a professor of management and organizations at Northwestern University's Kellogg School of Management. "You definitely want somebody leading it who people can look at and say, 'OK, we believe this is a report that we can fully believe and trust that the outcome is the right outcome,'" King said. "That's what investors are looking for. They just don't like the instability that comes with all of this." King said the Nvidia investigation sits at a unique intersection of Wall Street and Washington, where the company is likely navigating its next steps to try to appease both groups. sources.title: The US is winning the AI race. Jensen Huang could have blown it
sources.text: Nvidia’s chips are powering America’s AI boom. Of course Chinese spies are interested. Nvidia’s chips are powering America’s AI boom. Of course Chinese spies are interested. As espionage targets go, Jensen Huang is perhaps one of the least surprising on Earth. The Nvidia CEO runs one of the world’s most valuable companies, controls the in-demand technology fueling the AI boom, and is cozy with presidents, CEOs, and all manner of important people. He also wears a cool leather jacket. Which makes Huang’s admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy — reportedly while her spying was known to US intelligence and even President Donald Trump — all the more shocking. The fallout goes well beyond his marriage, his reputation, or Nvidia itself. Experts tell The Verge the incident threatens to disrupt the entire US AI industry, potentially jeopardize national security, and could undermine America’s efforts to maintain its fragile technological lead over China in AI. “With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.” Nvidia is the undisputed leader in advanced computer chips, among the AI industry’s scarcest resources. While many ingredients go into building AI models — including talent, energy, capital, and data — top-tier chips are one of the most important, and Nvidia is one of a handful of companies with the expertise to design or manufacture them at the cutting edge. That makes it a gatekeeper to hardware that has become a key bottleneck in global AI development. US companies — including Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI — are racing to develop chips of their own, in part to reduce their dependence on Nvidia, even as they spend billions securing ever more compute. For China, the US’s main rival at the frontier of AI, that bottleneck is even tighter. To maintain its technological lead, the US has restricted the sale of the most advanced AI chips to the country in the hopes of slowing its progress in the sector, which has been impressive and is thought to trail the US by a matter of months. In response, China has made developing domestic alternatives a strategic national priority, though its leaders still lag Nvidia at the bleeding edge. At the same time, a thriving black market for restricted Nvidia chips has emerged. Experts tell The Verge that China could exploit access to Nvidia to accelerate its own development, or to impede the US development of AI. Getting its hands on more Nvidia chips is the most obvious win for Beijing, says Emily Kilcrease, a senior fellow and director of the energy, economics, and security program at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) think tank. China has advantages in other parts of the AI race — including abundant energy and a solid ecosystem of open weight models — but without the latest Nvidia chips, it “cannot close the gap with US frontier capabilities,” Kilcrease tells The Verge . “With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.” It is not clear how successful the alleged spying operation has been on that front. There is no public evidence indicating that Huang himself has helped direct restricted Nvidia chips toward China or that sensitive information about them was obtained from him. But companies linked to the alleged spy, Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — have reportedly enabled at least $7 billion of Nvidia chip sales to China. Brookings fellow Kyle Chan tells The Verge that a concern for US industry could be that companies with alleged ties to China may have had priority access to Nvidia’s latest GPUs. “In a time of chip scarcity,” that would make it much harder for American companies to access them, Chan says. Huang is also a prominent critic of American restrictions on chip sales, and Nvidia spends a formidable amount lobbying in Washington. Last year, he successfully secured White House approval to start exporting Nvidia’s H200 AI GPU chips to “approved customers” in China and other countries. Crucially, Huang also has the ear of President Trump as well as other world leaders, giving him great influence over policy decisions. Hardware is not the only thing of value China could get from close access to Huang, Sunny Cheung, a fellow for China studies at the Jamestown Foundation think tank, tells The Verge . “I actually think too many people are focused on whether somebody managed to steal Nvidia’s trade secrets,” Cheung says, calling it a “very narrow way” of looking at espionage. “I would hope Jensen Huang isn’t foolish enough to hand over the blueprints for Nvidia’s next-generation chips to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.” The Nvidia CEO’s relationships with other tech executives, senior policymakers, and Trump himself give him an unusually intimate view into how some of the most powerful people in the US are thinking and planning. Beijing could use information on how American companies are planning major infrastructure expansions, their compute requirements, or broad industry trends to inform its own investments and industrial strategy, Cheung says. Huang’s intelligence value could extend well beyond AI, too. “That information alone could be extremely valuable,” says Cheung, pointing to insights Beijing could glean into White House thinking about export controls or the private views of Silicon Valley executives on China and Taiwan. “When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry.” But helping China advance is only one side of this equation. Disrupting Nvidia — as this scandal clearly has — could destabilize America’s entire AI industry. More than most companies, Nvidia is remarkably closely tied to the identity and reputation of its rockstar CEO. sources.title: Nvidia shares rebound as Jensen Huang faces scrutiny ahead of earnings
sources.text: Nvidia 's stock rose 3% on Wednesday, after falling for two days amid the scandal that has rocked the world's most valuable tech company. Shares closed down 5.47% on Tuesday as more details were revealed about the impact of CEO Jensen Huang 's affair with an alleged Chinese spy . They fell 4.3% Monday. On Tuesday, Nvidia announced it had hired law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate whether company secrets or national security were compromised. Huang tried to project "business as usual" as he returned to the office on Monday, people familiar with the matter told CNBC. The CEO was also in the office on Tuesday, conducting meetings, ahead of the company's quarterly earnings on Nov. 17. Investors are assessing whether the matter will have damaging spillover effects on the business. In a Tuesday note, Bank of America said it saw three scenarios with differing investment outcomes. In one scenario, the impact is contained with leadership continuity, and in another, prolonged uncertainty pressures valuation before earnings. In the final scenario, the impact is escalated, with "adverse findings, leadership disruption or tighter restrictions requiring earnings reassessment," BofA research analyst Vivek Arya said in the note. Zacks' Chief Equity Strategist John Blank said the selloff reflected two concerns: that the U.S. might impose further restrictions in the wake of the affair and that further problems might arise as the news develops. "What else has Jensen done?" he said. "It's not good for Nvidia. It's not good for Jensen Huang. It's certainly not good for the AI trade," Blank told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday. Morgan Stanley on Wednesday removed Nvidia as a top pick after shares dropped more than 25% since it was named on the list on Oct. 2. Huang's leadership is "crucial" to the company's strategic direction, analysts said in a Wednesday note. — CNBC's Michael Bloom and Caleigh Keating contributed to this report.

sources.title: NVIDIA shareholders are suing the company and CEO Jensen Huang
sources.text: The company’s shares have plummeted in response to the exec’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The unfolding drama around NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman now accused of being a spy for the Chinese government may be getting its first courtroom chapter. A shareholder in the computing giant has sued accusing NVIDIA and Huang of misleading investors about the nature of the CEO's relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Taiwanese company Megaspeed who is now suspected of being an espionage asset for China. Huang is a common surname; The pair are not related. Mark Kistenmacher filed the complaint and is seeking class action status for anyone who purchased NVIDIA shares between October 9 and November 8. The first date is when The New York Times published a story on NVIDIA and Megaspeed detailing a connection between the pair, which was rebuffed by NVIDIA as a routine business relationship; the second date is when the NVIDIA founder admitted to an affair and the company publicly disclosed that it was launching its own investigation into whether its top exec had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. In the interim, The New York Times published an in-depth feature on October 29 claiming that the NVIDIA CEO had become the subject of a suspected Chinese intelligence action. The piece cites NVIDIA representative John Rizzo, who said, "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." This statement, the lawsuit alleges, was not true. The company's shares have dropped in the fallout of the allegations, with NVIDIA on track to lose more than $470 billion in market value over the past two days. "As a result of Defendants' wrongful acts and omissions, and the precipitous decline in the market value of the Company's securities, Plaintiff and other Class members have suffered significant losses and damages," the complaint states.

sources.title: Anthropic sets a $1.4 trillion IPO target, but bankers may already be aiming higher
sources.text: Good morning. Anthropic set a proposed IPO valuation of up to roughly $1.4 trillion, below earlier reported expectations, but strong investor demand may already be pushing it higher. In an amended SEC filing on Tuesday, the Claude maker said it plans to offer 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 apiece in its proposed initial public offering. At the top of that range, the shares would have a combined value of approximately $64.35 billion. The offering includes shares sold by existing shareholders, from which Anthropic will receive no proceeds. Separately, Google, Nvidia , AMD , Broadcom , Micron , Microsoft and TSMC Partners, an affiliate of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, have agreed to purchase a combined $26 billion of Anthropic’s nonvoting Class N common stock through a private placement immediately following the IPO, according to the filing. That would bring the combined total to as much as $90.4 billion. Just weeks ago, reports had put the company’s potential valuation at roughly $2 trillion. Now, Anthropic’s bankers are considering pricing shares above the filed range, which could lift the valuation to $1.5 trillion or more, the Financial Times reported . Anthropic, which plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT, launched its roadshow on Tuesday, and the deal is expected to price on Nov. 18. CFO Krishna Rao , who joined Anthropic in 2024, is not selling any shares in the IPO. According to the filing, he beneficially owned about 9.5 million Class A shares as of Sept. 30, nearly all of it in stock options. At the top of the proposed range, that stake would have a gross value of roughly $740.8 million, before the cost of exercising the options and taxes. Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., wrote in a Tuesday note that the deal sets up a debate over “margin against growth,” with the stock likely to trade on whether Anthropic’s second-quarter operating profit or its third-quarter loss reflects its true run rate. Ives also argued that a more conservative valuation could help Anthropic achieve a successful market debut. The $1.4 trillion figure includes stock options and other equity awards. Counting only shares outstanding, he noted, the top of the range values the company at about $1 trillion. “Given the volatility and nervousness across the tech trade over the past week, we believe pricing at roughly $1 trillion, with the option to move toward $1.2 trillion if the book allows, is the right move,” Ives wrote. “A deal of this size gets one shot at its debut, and making it digestible for the market matters more than the last turn of valuation.” Sheryl Estrada Sheryl.Estrada@fortune.com Andrew Murray was named CFO of Albertsons ( No.57 ), effective Jan. 17. Murray succeeds Cody Perdue, who has served as interim CFO since Sept. 30 and will continue as SVP of treasury, investor relations and risk management. Murray joins Albertsons from Fonterra Co-operative Group, the world's largest dairy exporter, where he has been group CFO since 2024. He also oversees strategy, M&A, transformation and IT there. Before Fonterra, Murray was CFO of Simplot Australia, led global finance transformation at Toll Group, and held senior finance roles at Mondelez International. Dziadzio succeeds Jim Quinn, who has been CFO since 2017 and moves into the newly created role of president and chief transformation officer. Most recently, Dziadzio was interim CFO of Sterling Check during its acquisition by First Advantage. Before that, he spent more than seven years as EVP and CFO of Assurant. Jacqueline Maxwell was named CFO of Prolink , a Cincinnati-based workforce solutions firm, the company announced. She succeeds Jennifer Prospero, who becomes chief administrative officer. Maxwell has been with Prolink since 2012, most recently as vice president and corporate controller. Before that, she was a controller at Mary L. Shiley, LLC. Prospero joined Prolink as interim CFO in March 2024 and was named CFO in January 2025. sources.text: Anthropic’s public offering is expected to make it one of the world’s most valuable publicly traded companies as soon as next week. Anthropic’s public offering is expected to make it one of the world’s most valuable publicly traded companies as soon as next week. Anthropic confirmed on Tuesday that its IPO could be one of the biggest ever, even while falling short of previous expectations. Its IPO price is expected to be between $70.00 and $78.00 per share, which would put its valuation as high as $1.4 trillion, according to the The New York Times . The Wall Street Journal reports that according to its sources, Anthropic is “aiming for its shares to start trading Thursday or Friday next week.” As Reuters notes, the Anthropic IPO was previously expected to be valued at as much as $2 trillion. As of last week, Anthropic’s rival OpenAI was valued at $1.25 trillion . Those lower expectations follow months of debate around AI safety , and what that means, while midterm election results showed souring public opinion toward AI companies and data center projects they’re heavily investing in. And that doesn’t even include this past weekend’s revelations about an alleged Chinese spy’s involvement with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . The initial public offering price is expected to be between $70.00 and $78.00 per share. Anthropic has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.”

sources.title: Anthropic's IPO is an investor referendum on AI
sources.text: $1.4 trillion valuation. $90 billion raised. That's Anthropic's best-case scenario for its upcoming initial public offering, according to its recent regulatory filing . It's now up to the AI startup and its bankers to drum up interest with investors during its IPO road show , which started yesterday. The AI startup expects to price shares between $70 and $78. An official go-public date hasn't been set, but the end of next week appears the likely candidate. One thing that's not up to chance: The investors that committed to buying $26 billion in Anthropic shares at its IPO price. The backers are some of the biggest names in the AI race, including Broadcom, Google, and Nvidia. It highlights an ongoing criticism of the industry relying too heavily on circular financing . BI's Joe Ciolli, author of the First Trade newsletter , unpacks the decision to make an AI-heavy private placement in conjunction with the IPO. Aropic's IPO is an investor referendum on AI. It's a chance for investors to either support (or avoid) a new, key bellwether for the AI industry. Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters. The last time the general public had its say on AI, things didn't go well for the tech. (See: midterms .) Granted, these are investors, not general voters. Their interest is less about data centers in their backyard and more about whether it's a business that'll keep the stock price going up after they buy it. Anthropic's IPO paperwork, which shows the soaring compute cost needed to keep revenue growing, doesn't necessarily make that an easy sell either. Brian Boland knows something about going public in a challenging market. He was a vice president at Facebook during its disastrous 2012 IPO. He spoke to BI's Stephen Council about that experience and the similarities he sees with Anthropic's looming IPO . Facebook (now Meta) eventually figured it out, but it took more than a year for it to recover and close above its IPO price. With so much riding on AI, the stakes are much higher this time around. It's unclear if the market could stomach an AI darling underperforming for that long. Regardless of Anthropic's IPO performance, one group ( besides early investors and employees ) is already coming out ahead. The startup has budgeted a staggering $41.5 million in legal fees for its IPO, nearly double what SpaceX planned during its record-breaking IPO.

stories.title: A New AI Tool From Google DeepMind Proved the Signal Protocol Is Secure
stories.summary: DeepMind researchers were able to formally verify that the widely used encryption protocol works as intended. Their stretch goal? Do the same for “all the software of the world.”

sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: A New AI Tool From Google DeepMind Proved the Signal Protocol Is Secure
sources.text: Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself. Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world's communications on platforms like the Signal app , Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind's formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code. More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn't have critical vulnerabilities. Before the AI era, it was incredibly time-consuming for people to describe the characteristics of software they wanted to prove, turn these summaries into formulas, and then develop the proof. Agentic AI can significantly cut down the time of the latter project, enabling analyses like DeepMind's Signal evaluation. But even this analysis was limited in scope—it did not, for example, formally verify the entire Signal mobile app—and DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process. “We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED. The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work. While the speed of the project was notable, the DeepMind researchers point out that they were able to get a head start to a degree because of some past formal verification work that the Signal Foundation has conducted. “While prior formal verification focused on smaller portions of the code, Google DeepMind's approach enables significant expansion,” Ehren Kret, Signal's chief technology officer, says in a statement. “As AI-driven security threats grow, rigorously verifying the Signal protocol implementation gives us even greater confidence in our code's privacy guarantees.” For critical services used in high-stakes settings, it would be a dream to be able to formally verify every code base and entire software supply chains. “If you can now verify the correctness of these implementations, then you can rest easy,” says Pushmeet Kohli, chief scientist at Google Cloud and DeepMind's vice president of research. “You can imagine banks, imagine all those other companies who rely on assurances and who worry about bugs who could now say, ‘I can prove these properties.’" The open question across the tech sector, though, is whether AI-automated formal verification can truly scale—and whether it can do so at a workable cost. DeepMind conducted the Signal analysis free of charge as a research project, and Google declined to share the cost of the analysis. The company also declined to comment on whether it has plans to release a commercial formal verification product or service. The researchers say that some of their crucial advancements are in developing a “human-AI collaboration process,” as Chaudhuri puts it, that allows agents to contribute and self-correct at almost every phase of the process while still seeking human input and review at key junctures. “We don’t want this sort of vibe world where AI is generating the goals and AI is generating the proofs and basically taking tests that are self-written," Chaudhuri says. “There’s a middle ground.”

sources.title: Google’s new AI tool just proved Signal encryption really works – here’s how
sources.text: With the aim of securing other vital systems, Google DeepMind plans to open-source its AlphaProof Code. Researchers at Google DeepMind used AI to formally verify portions of Signal ‘s underlying code — meaning they’ve mathematically proven that at least part s of the encrypted messaging app’s code do what they say, without errors. That’s reassuring given how many vulnerabilities AI systems have discovered in software lately , and how many people’s communications are protected by Signal’s cryptography. WhatsApp and Google Messages use the same encryption. Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain DeepMind used AlphaProof Code, “a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents,” the researchers said. They added that formal verification “is the highest standard of security assurance,” but, without automation at scale like AI systems, difficult and time-consuming. AI companies like OpenAI have been on a math-breakthrough tear as of late, in some cases solving nearly century-old math problems with AI. By computing at such vast scale, AI models can rapidly accelerate much of the manual work mathematicians do. (Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.) Using AlphaProof Code and building on earlier verification work by the Signal Foundation, DeepMind researchers divided the verification task into two camps. Humans worked with agents to identify what they needed to prove, and multiple agents running Gemini Carbon, the company’s latest model, then executed it. The agents also audited the proof and “highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human — just 1% of the codebase, a massive time savings,” the researchers wrote. Also: After the vibe-coding rush comes the debugging hangover For good measure, researchers tested AlphaProof Code’s ability to distinguish correct from flawed code by showing it two previously fixed Signal bugs, for which it produced correct proofs. “Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth,” the researchers wrote. “It’s also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI.” Normally, researchers need to manually develop a proof to verify software, which takes much longer. That labor-intensive barrier has made formal verification a distant promised land, until now. The DeepMind team’s verification took a month to do what might normally take experts years. DeepMind did not verify all of Signal’s code, but noted that this test is a step toward improved security infrastructure at a time when AI is disrupting the entire cybersecurity space. Also: How to encrypt emails in Gmail, Outlook, and more “Having the core Signal protocol rigorously verified with automated theorem proving gives us even greater confidence that our code delivers on its privacy guarantees,” the researchers wrote. The breakthrough reiterates how deeply AI is both a massive risk for cybersecurity and an equally powerful fix. The year 2026 has been especially marked by AI-related security incidents, many of which involve agents. At the same time, companies like Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI are developing models geared specifically toward cybersecurity, including Anthropic’s Claude Mythos. Also: How to easily encrypt your files on an Android phone DeepMind did not share any plans to release its findings as a consumer product, though the researchers are open-sourcing their code to help others with formal verification efforts. “Verifying Signal’s core cryptography lays the groundwork to secure other vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software,” DeepMind added Please accept cookies to view the comments powered by Disqus.

sources.title: Claude can now join your weekly meeting to take notes and even start work for you — and that's not all, with new spreadsheet, whiteboard tools and more helping conquer the world of "Frontier Work"
sources.text: Anthropic wants Claude to help with "work at the frontier" Anthropic has unveiled a host of updates for Claude which could see the AI platform play a much more integral role in some of your most common work tasks. Among the next expansions are tools which allow Claude to join video calls as a participant, meaning it learns first-hand from your meetings and can start work immediately. Joining its existing suite of office software tools are new Whiteboards, Sheets and Data services looking to help users work and create more effectively - and new interactive connectors will now allow Claude to work inside the full versions of common workplace apps such as Adobe , Atlassian and HubSpot. "A year ago, Claude changed how developers work," Anthropic wrote in a blog post announcing the new tools. "Engineers stopped asking AI for snippets and started handing it whole tasks, which freed them to spend their time deciding what to build. For most other teams, work has stayed much the same: the email gets written a little faster, the meeting comes with a summary." "Now the frontier is moving to knowledge work, and people are starting to hand Claude whole tasks too." The most striking new addition is undoubtedly Claude Meetings, which will allow Claude to join video calls as a visible participant. Claude follows the conversation and starts on the work as people talk, taking notes, drafting plans, outlining timelines on whiteboards, answering chat questions, and utilizing connected work apps while conversations happen - and when the call ends, the notes, action items and everything Claude made are waiting in claude.ai. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! Also new is Claude Whiteboards, a shared, real-time board which helps teams turn brainstorms and retrospectives into structured plans, timelines, and action items, and integrates directly into Claude Meetings, and Claude Sheets, a spreadsheet tool which allows teams to build and edit trackers and budgets collaboratively with Claude, complete with tabs, formulas, and dropdown menus. Finally, Claude Data (formerly known as Claude Dashboards) connects company data sources (such as CRMs and warehouses) to generate dashboards, data stories, and narrated videos, featuring beta capabilities like certified queries and live sharing. Alongside this, new Interactive Connectors will allow full versions of partner tools (like Adobe, Atlassian, HubSpot, Salesforce , NetSuite, and Workday) to open directly inside Claude, which can take actions directly within these apps with user approval. Connectors respect existing user permissions, and admins can utilize features like Claude auto-connect, usage controls, and Smart Reports to monitor team productivity and costs. Claude Meetings, Claude Whiteboard and Claude Sheets are all still in beta, with Claude Data and Interactive Connectors generally available now. sources.name: Hipertextual
sources.title: La amante de Jensen Huang habría ayudado a desviar 7.500 millones de dólares en chips de NVIDIA a China
sources.text: La aventura extramatrimonial de Jensen Huang con la supuesta espía china Alice Huang no solo está ocupando titulares en todo el mundo, sino que ha disparado tanto una revisión interna de NVIDIA como una investigación del FBI. Y las implicaciones del escándalo amoroso son cada vez más notorias. Según reporta The Information , la relación entre Jensen Huang y Alice Huang dataría al menos desde 2023. Pero no solo eso, sino que la amante del CEO de NVIDIA habría ayudado a desviar unos 7.500 millones de dólares en chips avanzados hacia el gigante asiático , a pesar del bloqueo de Estados Unidos . El citado medio indica que Alice Huang habría montado una red de empresas en China y Singapur junto con su esposo y su hermana, destacando una firma llamada Shanghai Century Litong. Esta se fundó en junio de 2023 y apenas meses después, en octubre, se convirtió en socio preferente de NVIDIA para servicios en la nube. Ser socio preferente de NVIDIA le daba a la compañía acceso prioritario a sus chips. No obstante, la situación se habría complicado tras la entrada en vigor del veto de Estados Unidos a la exportación de hardware avanzado para servidores de IA hacia China. No obstante, Alice Huang habría sacado provecho de su cercanía con Jensen Huang para mover hilos y evadir el bloqueo . Puntualmente, The Information indica que Alice Huang habría utilizado sus vínculos con NVIDIA y los distribuidores de la empresa para garantizarse el acceso a sus chips avanzados y enviarlos a China. Se menciona en tal sentido que la estrategia habría facilitado el envío de 240.000 placas gráficas H100, H200 y A100 hacia el gigante asiático . Así, se estima que la amante de Jensen Huang habría logrado movilizar hardware por al menos 7.500 millones de dólares desde 2023. El culebrón por la relación entre Jensen Huang y Alice Huang está muy lejos de finalizar. La historia se destapó a finales de octubre, cuando The New York Times publicó que el CEO de NVIDIA mantenía una "relación cercana" con la presunta espía china . El citado medio no explicitó si se trataba de un vínculo romántico, pero las especulaciones no se hicieron esperar. El reporte original sostenía que Jensen Huang no sabía que Alice Huang estaba enviando información hacia China. También decía que Donald Trump conocía sobre el tema desde hacía un año, pero que había optado por no tomar cartas en el asunto. En una conferencia de prensa que realizó ayer en la Casa Blanca , el presidente de EE. UU. dijo que el jefe de NVIDIA le confesó que no estaba al tanto de que su amante era una espía china. Si bien NVIDIA negó inicialmente que el vínculo entre Jensen Huang y Alice Huang fuese problemático, la historia cambió en los últimos días. El domingo, el propio líder y fundador de la empresa reconoció haber tenido una relación extramatrimonial , y la firma anunció la puesta en marcha de una investigación interna . Durante la jornada bursátil del lunes, la acción de NVIDIA cayó un 5 %. Así, la empresa perdió unos 190.000 millones de dólares de valor de mercado en un solo día . Al momento de redacción de este artículo, el gigante verde tiene un marketcap de 4,3 billones de dólares. Esto ha dejado a Apple como la única empresa del mundo que vale más de 5 billones de dólares.

sources.name: Xataka
sources.title: El escándalo de Jensen Huang iba a ser un problema para Jensen Huang. Va a acabar siendo un problema para los chips de NVIDIA
sources.text: El escándalo de espionaje que rodea a Jensen Huang está inclinando contra NVIDIA la pelea por los chips en el Congreso . Lo curioso es lo que podría salir de ahí. La medida con más opciones de aprobarse no toca a Huang, sino a sus chips, que tendrían que poder decir en todo momento dónde están. Qué ha ocurrido . Todo empezó cuando The New York Times contó que el espionaje chino tenía a Huang en el punto de mira . Días después él mismo admitió una relación extramatrimonial con Alice Huang, exdirectiva de la empresa singapurense Megaspeed. Según Trump, el FBI ya está investigando . Entre líneas . Si esto fuera solo una infidelidad, el asunto se quedaría en Jensen Huang y en su familia. Lo que lo complica es Megaspeed: era una gran compradora de chips de NVIDIA , y además opera desde Singapur, una de las rutas por las que esos chips acaban llegando a China. Ese es exactamente el agujero que quiere tapar la Chip Security Act . Obligaría a que los chips avanzados verifiquen su ubicación, y todo apunta a que entrará en la ley de defensa antes de que termine el año. En detalle . El sistema funcionaría midiendo la latencia . Con eso no se sabe la ubicación exacta de un chip, pero sí puede saberse si está en Singapur o en China, que es lo que interesa. NVIDIA se queja de que eso encarecerá el producto, si bien esta es la más suave de las tres propuestas que se están discutiendo. Punto de inflexión . Brian Mast, uno de los republicanos que están impulsando estos nuevos límites, cree que el escándalo ha debilitado “al 100%” la capacidad de Huang para frenarlos. Lo apoyan tanto el presidente de la Cámara, Mike Johnson, como el líder demócrata, Hakeem Jeffries. En el fondo es una ruptura con Trump, que llevaba un año facilitando las ventas a China. Sí, pero . NVIDIA ha dejado de hacer lobby a cara descubierta y ahora deja que hablen por ella sus grandes clientes, como OpenAI o Meta. El problema es que a muchos de ellos los controles les vienen estupendamente. A Microsoft o Amazon, por ejemplo, les dejarían más chips disponibles, rivales chinos más débiles y mejor posición para negociar con NVIDIA. Y ahora qué . Huang comparecerá a puerta cerrada el 18 de noviembre , de forma voluntaria, mientras NVIDIA únicamente está investigando si filtró secretos . Es posible que salga bien parado. Pero si el rastreo acaba en la ley, se quedará en los chips de NVIDIA mucho después de que el escándalo se haya olvidado.
